At the same time, Sylphie ignores her parents' warning and approaches a natural treasure guarded by Goldsun Eagles. Their level-144 Prima nearly kills Hawkie and Mystie before Jake arrives, heals the family, and defeats the attacker. Rather than execute it himself, he leaves the final decision to the hawks. Sylphie kills it as an acceptance of responsibility for endangering her family. The victory yields the second Key Fragment of the Exalted Prima, while Jake also secures an ancient sun-affinity fragment.

Sylphie reaches level 100 and evolves into a half-elemental bird. The primordial elemental Stormild offers her a divine blessing and a union oath with Jake. Jake rejects a conventional lifelong companion bond, and his bloodline refuses to accept Stormild as a superior judge. With power drawn through the Malefic Viper, the oath changes into an equal agreement without Stormild's enforcement and will fade naturally within decades. Jake then sends Sylphie to train alone, requiring her to reach level 110 and prove she can avoid rescue if she wants to enter the treasure hunt.

Arnold returns Jake's upgraded Nanoblade and uses Jake's perception to help map the microscopic structure of Altmar material. Jake transforms Sultan's fire-based bow into an epic, quasi-soulbound arcane weapon suited to his arrows. He continues brewing uncommon elixirs, reaches race and profession level 129, and finally uses his awakening token on the Boots of the Wandering Alchemist, turning them into epic equipment with improved movement and sensitivity to natural treasures.

Neil and his full party reach D-grade in time to qualify for the treasure hunt. Miranda continues directing Haven and supervises the surviving captive who chose Haven, while Sultan hunts with the woman who chose to remain under his contract. Phillip admits that burnout and loss of purpose have stopped his advancement at level 99, so he begins preparing a successor to command the fort's soldiers. Jake spends the last days supplying Haven's eligible entrants with elixirs, poisons, and potions. Sylphie is training independently under her limited equal oath with Jake, Hawkie and Mystie remain alive, and Sultan continues under Haven's restrictions. The book ends shortly before the treasure hunt, with Jake prepared to enter and expecting his arranged fight with Miyamoto.

characters.description: The Lion of Narnia, known to the reader from the earlier book: the country's maker and true king, who comes and goes as he chooses and is not at anyone's command. At the opening of this story he has not been seen in Narnia for a very long time, and most of its people no longer believe he was ever real.
characters.name: Aslan

characters.description: The eldest of the four children and once High King of Narnia. Back in England he is an ordinary schoolboy again, but he takes responsibility as a matter of course, and expects to be obeyed when a decision has to be made quickly.
characters.name: Peter Pevensie

characters.description: The elder sister, once Queen Susan of Narnia and a formidable archer. Sensible and comfort-loving, she is the one who argues for the safe and reasonable course, and she is slower than the others to trust anything that cannot be seen plainly.
characters.name: Susan Pevensie

characters.description: The younger brother, once King Edmund of Narnia. Quiet, observant and steady, he has learned from being badly wrong once before and is quick to back his sister Lucy when the others will not.
characters.name: Edmund Pevensie

characters.description: The youngest of the four and once Queen Lucy of Narnia. She is the readiest of them to believe in Narnia and the most delighted to be back, and she notices things the others miss, which is not always comfortable for anyone.
characters.name: Lucy Pevensie

characters.description: A Red Dwarf of Old Narnia, found bound and about to be drowned by soldiers. Tough, dry and disbelieving by temperament, he calls himself a sceptic about lions and magic while serving his king loyally and going wherever he is sent. He is a good shot, a good swordsman and a good storyteller.
characters.name: Trumpkin

characters.description: The young heir of the Telmarine line, brought up in his uncle's castle and taught by his nurse that the old Narnia of Talking Beasts and dryads was real. He is eager, well-meaning and largely untested, and he loves the stories his tutor and his nurse tell him more than the court he lives in.
characters.name: Prince Caspian

characters.description: Caspian's tutor, a small stout scholar who turns out to be partly of dwarf blood and to have kept the old learning alive in secret. He teaches Caspian real Narnian history at night on the castle roof and takes considerable risks to protect him.
characters.name: Doctor Cornelius

characters.description: Caspian's uncle, who governs Telmarine Narnia as Lord Protector and then as king. Cold, capable and thorough, he has stamped out talk of Old Narnia, keeps the woods and the sea feared and unvisited, and disposes quietly of anyone in his way.
characters.name: King Miraz

characters.description: A Talking Badger of Old Narnia, one of the creatures living hidden in the woods. Slow, obstinate and long-memoried, he insists that badgers do not forget and that a son of Adam belongs on Narnia's throne, and he is the first to argue for accepting Caspian.
characters.name: Trufflehunter

characters.description: A Black Dwarf living in hiding with Trufflehunter and Trumpkin, bitter about what the Telmarines have done to his people and suspicious of every human alive. Finding a Telmarine boy asleep in his cave, his first proposal is to kill him rather than risk trusting him.
characters.name: Nikabrik

characters.description: A Talking Mouse about a foot high, immaculately courteous, ferociously brave and touchy about his honour and his size. He leads a company of mice and is among the first of the Old Narnians to offer Caspian his sword.
characters.name: Reepicheep

characters.description: A centaur, a prophet and a star-gazer, who reads the coming war in the movements of the planets and brings his sons to Caspian's muster. Grave and formal, he is the most impressive of the Old Narnians to declare for the prince.
characters.name: Glenstorm

characters.description: A Telmarine lord of Miraz's council, watchful and careful never to say what he thinks in the open. He has been ill-used by the king and remembers it.
characters.name: Lord Glozelle

recaps.ending: Peter fights Miraz in single combat before both armies while Aslan, with Susan and Lucy, wakes the woods and the rivers behind them. Miraz stumbles, and two of his own lords stab him and shout that the Narnians have murdered him, so the Telmarine army charges. The woken trees and the Old Narnians rout it, and the retreat over the river is cut off because Aslan has thrown down the bridge at Beruna. Caspian is confirmed as King Caspian the Tenth, with Doctor Cornelius as his counsellor and Trumpkin as Lord Regent, and Aslan tells him he will do well because he knows he is not fit for it. Aslan spends the following days restoring the country: freeing prisoners, healing the sick, and putting an end to the schools and towns where fear of the woods was taught. He then explains the Telmarines' own history, which they had lost: they came originally from our world, pirates who fell through a gap on an island in the South Seas. He opens a door in the air, and those who wish to leave Narnia pass through it into an empty country of our world where they may start again. The children go home through the same door, and Peter and Susan are told privately that they are now too old to return to Narnia. They arrive back on the railway platform with their luggage, a few seconds after they left.
recaps.in_short: A year after coming home from Narnia, the four Pevensie children are pulled off an English railway platform into a wood, and find that they are on an island that was once the headland of Cair Paravel, their own ruined castle. Centuries have passed in Narnia. They rescue a dwarf, Trumpkin, who tells them that Telmarine invaders have ruled for generations and driven the Talking Beasts into hiding, and that the rightful heir, Prince Caspian, has fled his usurping uncle Miraz and raised the Old Narnians in revolt. Besieged, Caspian blew Queen Susan's magic horn, which is what brought the children back. Journeying to join him, the party goes astray because only Lucy can see Aslan, and they follow him at last only after losing a day and a fight. Aslan wakes the woods; Peter challenges Miraz to single combat; Miraz is murdered by his own lords, and the Telmarine army is broken by the trees and cut off at the ruined bridge. Caspian is crowned, the Telmarines are offered a passage back to the world their pirate ancestors came from, and the children return to England, where Peter and Susan learn they are too old to come back.

recaps.text: Peter, Susan, Edmund and Lucy Pevensie, four children sent out of wartime London, once found their way into Narnia through a wardrobe in an old professor's house. There they met the Lion Aslan, who broke the White Witch's spell of endless winter at the cost of his own life and returned alive, and the four were crowned kings and queens at Cair Paravel. They ruled for many years, grew up, and then rode back through the wood after a white stag and tumbled out of the wardrobe as children again, with no time at all having passed at home. A year of English time has gone by since. Narnian time runs at its own rate and quite independently of ours, so there is no telling from this side how long it has been there.

Waiting on a country railway platform at the end of the holidays, the four children feel themselves pulled sideways out of England and land in a wood by the sea. They find fresh water and fruit, and discover they are on a small island. Exploring a ruin among the trees, they slowly realise what it is: the island was once a headland, and the ruin is Cair Paravel, their own castle. The treasure chamber beneath it is still sealed, and their gifts are still there, Peter's sword and shield, Susan's bow and quiver, Lucy's cordial that heals any wound. Susan's horn is missing, left behind on the day they rode after the white stag. Centuries must have passed in Narnia since they left. Looking out at the water, they see a boat with two soldiers rowing a bound dwarf out to drown him, and they scatter the soldiers with an arrow shot and a rush, and bring the dwarf ashore.

The dwarf, Trumpkin, tells them what has happened to Narnia. Telmarines from the west conquered the country generations ago, drove the Talking Beasts, dwarfs and tree-spirits into hiding, and taught that they never existed, fearing the woods and the sea and letting the coast go wild. The heir, Prince Caspian, was brought up by his uncle King Miraz, who had murdered Caspian's father to take the throne. Caspian's nurse told him the old stories and was dismissed for it; his new tutor, Doctor Cornelius, secretly half a dwarf, taught him at night that Old Narnia was real and still hiding in the woods. When a son was born to Miraz, Cornelius woke Caspian in the small hours, gave him Queen Susan's lost horn, and sent him away for his life. Caspian rode for the woods, was knocked from his horse in a storm, and woke in a cave being argued over by a badger and two dwarfs.

Trufflehunter the badger, who holds that a son of Adam belongs on the throne, wins the argument over the suspicious dwarf Nikabrik, and Caspian is taken to meet the hidden creatures of Old Narnia one by one: bears, mice under the mouse Reepicheep, a company of centaurs under the star-gazer Glenstorm, giants, fauns, and less reputable folk as well. Doctor Cornelius arrives with the news that Miraz's army is on the march. At a great council Caspian is accepted as king, and the war begins badly: the Old Narnians are beaten back and besieged at Aslan's How, the mound raised long ago over the Stone Table. With supplies failing, Caspian is persuaded to blow Susan's horn and ask for help, though no one knows what form it will take. Messengers are sent to meet whatever comes, and Trumpkin, who believes in none of it, volunteers for the Cair Paravel road. He was captured on the way, which is how he came to be in the boat.

Trumpkin, having tested Susan's shooting and Edmund's swordplay and been beaten at both, accepts that the four are who they say and agrees to guide them to Aslan's How. They row round the coast and up the Glasswater creek, then strike inland through country that has changed out of recognition in the centuries since they knew it. At a gorge the route is disputed. Lucy sees Aslan standing among the trees on the far side, beckoning them upward and away from the river; nobody else can see him, and the others vote against her and take the easier downhill way. It leads them into arrow fire from a Telmarine post at the ford, and they lose a day struggling back the way they came.

In the night Lucy wakes, finds Aslan, and is told that she must follow him even if the others will not come. She wakes them; they come, grumbling. As they go, one after another begins to see him, Edmund first, then Peter, then Susan, and last of all Trumpkin, who is picked up and shaken like a toy before he is set down again as a believer. Aslan leads them along the gorge in the dark to Aslan's How, sends Peter, Edmund and Trumpkin inside to deal with what is happening there, and then roars. The woods wake; trees come loose from their places and follow him, and Bacchus, Silenus and their wild company arrive to join the girls at his side.

Inside the dark mound Peter and Edmund arrive in the middle of an argument. Nikabrik, out of patience with waiting for a lion out of old stories, has brought in a hag and a werewolf and is urging Caspian to call the White Witch back from the dead, on the grounds that her power at least was real and lasted a hundred years. Caspian, Trufflehunter and Doctor Cornelius refuse, the lamps go out, and in the fight in the dark Nikabrik, the hag and the werewolf are killed. Peter takes command of the war. Rather than let the Old Narnians be worn down by a larger army, he sends Edmund with a formal challenge to Miraz for single combat, to settle the quarrel between the two of them. Miraz is inclined to refuse, but two of his own lords, Glozelle and Sopespian, taunt him into accepting for reasons of their own.

Peter and Miraz fight before both armies. Miraz stumbles over a tussock, and Glozelle and Sopespian stab him where he lies and shout that the Narnians have killed him under a truce, sending the Telmarine army into the attack. The woken trees come down on them and the army breaks; the survivors run for the river and find the bridge at Beruna gone, thrown down by Aslan and the river god, and are penned against the water and surrender. Caspian is made king, with Cornelius as his counsellor and Trumpkin as Lord Regent. Aslan spends the next days going through the country, freeing the ill-treated, healing the sick and ending the fearful schooling of the towns, and then tells the Telmarines what they had forgotten: their ancestors were pirates from our world who fell through a gap on a South Sea island. He opens a door in the air; those who choose it pass through to an empty country of our world to begin again. The children go through the same door and land back on the railway platform, and Peter and Susan are told privately that they are now too old ever to return to Narnia.

characters.description: Chicago's professional wizard, now wearing the gray cloak of a Warden of the White Council - a bitter irony for a man the Wardens once wanted to execute. The vampire war drags on, the Council is stretched to breaking, and Harry opens the book forced to witness the execution of a teenage warlock, the Council's justice at its most merciless. When word reaches him that black magic is moving in Chicago, the hunt leads somewhere that tests every loyalty he has - and what he does about it will put his own neck under the sword.
characters.name: Harry Dresden

characters.description: The most enigmatic member of the Senior Council, keeper of the Outer Gates. After the execution that opens the book, Rashid quietly points Harry at a problem: traces of black magic in Chicago that the Council's own resources have not run down. His hints are sparse and deliberate, as if he already knows more than he can say, and his trust in Harry - rare among the Council's leadership - carries its own weight of expectation.
characters.name: Rashid

characters.description: Harry's half-brother, the White Court vampire, still nominally sharing Harry's apartment but increasingly absent and evasive about where his money and time are going. Whatever he is hiding, his loyalty is not in question: when Harry mounts the most dangerous rescue of his life, Thomas is beside him without being asked.
characters.name: Thomas Raith

characters.description: Michael and Charity Carpenter's eldest child, no longer the kid Harry remembers: a tall teenager in piercings, dye, and deliberate defiance of her mother's household, halfway out the door of her family's faith. Molly calls Harry when her boyfriend is arrested after a bizarre attack at a horror convention, and pulls him into the case. She is smart, stubborn, and carrying more than she tells anyone.
characters.name: Molly Carpenter

characters.description: Karrin Murphy, of Chicago PD's Special Investigations - paying the price for standing with Harry: her unexplained absences have cost her the command of SI, a demotion she absorbs without complaint and without an ounce of regret. Off the org chart or on it, she remains Harry's steadiest ally, and she walks into Faerie itself beside him.
characters.name: Karrin Murphy

characters.description: Michael's wife and the iron center of the Carpenter household, whose long hostility toward Harry has never softened. This case drives into her deepest fears and oldest secrets: Charity was not always a knight's wife baking bread for seven children, and what she gave up - and why - turns out to matter enormously to what is happening now. Her love for her children is a force of nature.
characters.name: Charity Carpenter

characters.description: The shadow of the fallen angel Lasciel, resident in Harry's mind since he grabbed her coin, now an acknowledged - and dangerously useful - presence. She offers recall, translation, tactical help, and access to hellfire that puts real weight behind Harry's magic, all in the tone of a perfectly agreeable companion. Every gift is a payment on the same patient investment: the day Harry digs up the coin.
characters.name: Lasciel's shadow

characters.description: Once a changeling waitress Harry saved from the Stone Table, now the Summer Lady, youngest queen of the Summer Court, with her friend Fix elevated beside her as the Summer Knight. Lily receives Harry with genuine warmth and owes him a debt she has not forgotten, but her office binds what she may say and do; her careful, constrained help - and what she cannot tell him about the strange behavior of Winter - shapes Harry's understanding of the storm gathering between the Courts.
characters.name: Lily

characters.description: The onetime nervous changeling mechanic, now the Summer Knight - the Summer Court's mortal champion, grown into a wiry confidence that sits strangely on Harry's memory of him. Fix serves Lily with total devotion, and like her he is bound in what he may reveal. His transformation since the Stone Table is a quiet reminder of what the Courts' power does to the mortals who take it up.
characters.name: Fix

characters.description: The greatest of the fetches sent out of Winter: a towering shape-shifting horror that wears the forms of fear itself. The Scarecrow leads the phobophages - spirit predators that take the shapes of horror-movie monsters and feed on terror - hunting a specific quarry in Chicago, and it is strong enough to go through a Warden of the White Council to get there. It answers to power deep inside Arctis Tor, Winter's capital.
characters.name: The Scarecrow

recaps.ending: The black magic in Chicago was Molly Carpenter's: her talent woke, and out of love she used mind-altering magic on two friends to force them off drugs - twice breaking one of the Laws of Magic, and drawing the attention of Winter, whose fetches hunted her through the horror convention and finally carried her to Arctis Tor. Harry, Charity, Murphy and Thomas raid Winter's capital to bring her back, finding its gates already blasted by someone else's hellfire and the Leanansidhe imprisoned in ice beneath Mab's fountain; they rescue Molly, and the pursuing Scarecrow is destroyed at the threshold of the mortal world with Summer's help. Then comes the harder fight: before the White Council, the Merlin is ready to execute Molly as a warlock. Harry stakes his own life on her - she is placed under the Doom of Damocles as his apprentice, her death sentence suspended so long as she stays clean, with Harry's falling with hers if she does not. Michael's family is shaken but intact, and Charity's secret - that she once wielded magic herself and abandoned it - is out. Murphy has been demoted to sergeant for standing with Harry, and accepts it. The war's larger shape darkens: the attack on Arctis Tor, the Council's stretched forces, and a suspicion Harry can no longer dismiss - that a traitor moves within the Council, and that some organized hand is behind years of supposedly separate catastrophes. Molly moves through Harry's door as his student, and the book closes with teacher and apprentice facing a long road.
recaps.in_short: Now a reluctant Warden, Harry witnesses a teenage warlock's execution, then is pointed at traces of black magic in Chicago. When Molly Carpenter's boyfriend is arrested at a horror convention, Harry finds phobophages - fear-eating shapeshifters out of Winter - attacking the con in the forms of movie monsters, and the trail of the black magic and the trail of the fetches converge on Molly herself: her awakened talent, used with the best intentions to mind-alter friends off drugs, has made her a warlock in the Council's eyes and Winter's prey. The fetches kidnap her to Arctis Tor; Harry, Charity (whose own abandoned magic is her buried secret), Murphy and Thomas raid Winter's capital - finding it already scarred by someone else's hellfire attack - and bring her home, destroying the Scarecrow. Before the Council, Harry saves Molly from execution by taking her as his apprentice under the shared Doom of Damocles. Murphy is demoted for her loyalty; the evidence of a traitor inside the Council hardens; and Harry begins training the girl whose life now depends on him.

recaps.text: Previously: Harry Dresden broke the Darkhallow - three necromancer disciples of Heinrich Kemmler warring to become a god on Halloween night - by riding a reanimated museum T. rex into battle, with the timid medical examiner Waldo Butters drumming the spell's beat. Grevane and the body-stealing Corpsetaker died; the hooded Cowl vanished unconfirmed; and Warden-Captain Luccio was left permanently in a stranger's young body. The gutted White Council drafted Harry into the Wardens as a regional commander. He carries hidden costs: the shadow of the fallen angel Lasciel lives in his mind, offering power against the day he digs up her buried coin; his left hand is burned and crippled; and his half-brother, the White Court vampire Thomas, shares his apartment. Karrin Murphy of Special Investigations knows his world and fights beside him. Molly, eldest child of Harry's friend Michael Carpenter, Knight of the Cross, is growing up fast. The war with the Red Court grinds on.

Harry's Warden cloak weighs heaviest at an execution: he stands witness as the Council beheads a teenage boy who used magic to enslave minds - the Laws of Magic applied without mercy, to children who often never knew the Laws existed. Afterward the Gatekeeper quietly sets him a task: something is working black magic in Chicago, and Harry should find it before the Wardens do. At home, the war news is grim and the Council's suspicions of a traitor in its ranks are growing. Then Molly Carpenter calls: her boyfriend Nelson has been arrested after a man was brutally attacked in a washroom at SplatterCon!!!, a horror-film convention - an attack with details no mundane assailant explains.

Harry works the convention and finds the truth worse than a haunting: phobophages, spirit predators that feed on fear, are manifesting in the shapes of the con's own movie monsters and attacking guests. The creatures are fetches - shapeshifters out of the Winter Court - and something is calling them to this place. Harry rigs wards, coordinates with Murphy and the SI-friendly officer Rawlins, and rides out a second night of attacks that turns bloody: people are hurt and killed, Harry is nearly overwhelmed, and the biggest of the fetches escapes back into the Nevernever. Along the way Harry notices what he least wants to see - the traces of black magic the Gatekeeper sent him hunting are here, tangled with the people around Molly.

Harry consults the Summer Court: Lily, the onetime changeling now Summer Lady, and Fix, the Summer Knight, receive him warmly but speak in careful circles - the Courts are moving strangely, Mab's behavior has Summer alarmed, and Winter's forces are massing in ways that make no sense if the fetches are mere raiders. Bound by her office, Lily cannot simply tell him what Winter is doing; what she can give him is context and a debt acknowledged. Meanwhile the fetches strike their real target: they take Molly. Harry establishes where she has been carried - Arctis Tor, Mab's own citadel, the frozen heart of Winter - and that no sane rescue is possible. Charity Carpenter, tearing the armor off her own past, reveals the secret under her hostility to wizards: she had power once, and a sorcerer she loved misused her for it; she gave up her talent, and Molly's inheritance of it is her oldest terror. With Michael away, the rescue party forms without a Knight: Harry, Charity in her husband's spare mail, Murphy, and Thomas.

The raid on Arctis Tor is Harry's deepest venture into Faerie. Winter's capital stands strangely quiet - its gates are blasted and its courtyard scorched with hellfire, the residue of an attack by some unknown third power that has already come and gone - and the Leanansidhe, Harry's godmother, is found imprisoned in the ice of Mab's fountain, her caretaking of Harry's debt claimed by Mab herself. The team fights through the citadel's remaining defenders to Molly, held by the Scarecrow and its fetches, and Harry burns through tricks, borrowed power, and the last of his strength to pull her out. The escape becomes a running battle: the Scarecrow pursues them between worlds, and is finally destroyed at the boundary of the mortal realm, with Summer's power turned against Winter's hunter. Molly is saved - and the source of the black magic in Chicago is now undeniable: it was Molly, her talent awakened, who twice bent her friends' minds to force them off drugs. Love was the motive; the Law is the Law.

Molly stands trial before the White Council as a warlock, and the Merlin - with the war bleeding the Council white and mercy in short supply - is prepared to execute her. Harry, who has spent the book watching what the Council's justice does to gifted children, puts his own life in the scale: Molly is granted the Doom of Damocles, her death sentence suspended, on the condition that she trains as Harry's apprentice - and that Harry answers for her with his head if she falls back into black magic. Michael returns to a family shaken but whole, Charity's secret now in the open between her and her daughter. Murphy's price also comes due: demoted to sergeant for her unexplained absences, she keeps her badge and her resolve. Harry closes the book with an apprentice in his lab, a growing certainty that a traitor inside the Council - and perhaps an organized 'Black Council' behind years of convenient catastrophes - is real, and the uneasy knowledge that the hellfire scars on Arctis Tor mean someone out there can make war on Mab herself.

characters.description: Pteppic, crown prince of the small, ancient river kingdom of Djelibeybi, sent abroad to be trained at the Assassins' Guild in Ankh-Morpork. Caught between his modern education and the weight of his homeland's seven thousand years of tradition, he is thoughtful and reluctant, more comfortable solving practical problems than playing the role of god-king he is about to inherit.
characters.name: Teppic

characters.description: A fellow student at the Assassins' Guild, the son of a wealthy merchant family, who becomes Teppic's closest friend during his training. Worldly and enterprising, he later helps Teppic when he needs allies from outside the kingdom.
characters.name: Chidder

characters.description: A gaunt, exacting examiner at the Assassins' Guild who conducts Teppic's final test, the practical examination that decides whether a student graduates as a qualified assassin.
characters.name: Mericet

characters.description: Teppic's father and the reigning god-king of Djelibeybi, worn down by the demands of divine rule and increasingly convinced that he is a seabird. His death sets the plot in motion, and his spirit remains uncomfortably conscious inside his own mummified body, distressed by the funerary rites performed upon it.
characters.name: King Teppicymon XXVII

characters.description: The high priest of Djelibeybi, an old man who has served the kingdom and its gods for longer than anyone can remember. He is the true power behind the throne, administering every ritual and custom with absolute devotion to tradition, and he expects the new king to be a figurehead who does as the rites require.
characters.name: Dios

characters.description: A handmaiden of the late king, spirited and outspoken, who under Djelibeybi's customs is to be entombed alive to serve the dead pharaoh. Teppic saves her from that fate, and she proves stubborn, practical, and unwilling to accept the kingdom's traditions without question.
characters.name: Ptraci

characters.description: The kingdom's master pyramid-builder, a businessman contracted to raise the enormous pyramid for the dead king. He works alongside his two sons, one an architect and one an accountant, and finds his trade colliding with the strange effects that pyramids unleash.
characters.name: Ptaclusp

characters.description: A camel of the kingdom who happens to be the greatest mathematician on the Disc, working through complex calculations in his head while appearing to do nothing but chew and spit.
characters.name: You Bastard

recaps.ending: Pyramids ends with Djelibeybi freed from the weight of its own past. Teppic and his allies determine that the enormous new Great Pyramid, which had twisted the kingdom out of reality, must be destroyed, and they collapse it to release its hoarded time. The pocket dimension unravels, the many gods that had become physically real disappear, and Djelibeybi returns to the ordinary world. Dios, the ancient high priest who had ruled through tradition and secretly renewed his own life inside the pyramids for millennia, is caught in the structure's last flare and thrown thousands of years back to the kingdom's founding, condemned to live out his service from the beginning again. Teppic, having become king, concludes that the kingdom cannot survive by clinging to its rituals. He steps down and hands the throne to Ptraci, the rescued handmaiden who proves to be his half-sister; as queen she opens Djelibeybi to trade and new ideas, ending its isolation and its age of pyramid-building. His father's restless spirit is finally laid to rest, and Teppic departs, leaving a kingdom beginning to rejoin the wider Disc.
recaps.in_short: Teppic, prince of the ancient river kingdom of Djelibeybi, trains as an assassin in cosmopolitan Ankh-Morpork, but on qualifying he learns that his father, the god-king, has died and he must return to take the throne. At home he finds true power held by Dios, the immensely old high priest who rules through rigid tradition. Pressed to build the largest pyramid ever for his dead father, Teppic clashes with Dios and rescues a condemned handmaiden, Ptraci. Djelibeybi's pyramids store time, and when the vast new pyramid flares it wrenches the whole kingdom out of the world into its own dimension, where every god the people ever believed in becomes real and runs riot. Teppic, caught outside, fights his way back and, with Ptraci and the builder Ptaclusp, destroys the Great Pyramid to bring the kingdom home. Dios is hurled into the distant past to repeat his service forever. Teppic abdicates in favour of Ptraci, his half-sister, who becomes queen and finally opens the kingdom to the modern world.

recaps.text: Teppic, prince of the ancient, tradition-bound river kingdom of Djelibeybi, is completing his training at the Assassins' Guild in the great city of Ankh-Morpork, far from home. He passes his final practical examination and qualifies as an assassin, having grown used to a modern, cosmopolitan world. On the same night, back in Djelibeybi, his father, King Teppicymon XXVII, dies, and Teppic learns that he must return home to take the throne as the kingdom's new god-king.

Home again, Teppic finds that real power lies with Dios, the ancient high priest who governs every act of the god-king according to unbreakable tradition. Teppic is expected to preside over his father's elaborate funeral and to commission the largest pyramid the kingdom has ever built, a project undertaken by the builder Ptaclusp and his sons. Meanwhile the dead king's spirit remains trapped and aware inside his mummified body. Teppic balks at one custom in particular and rescues a handmaiden, Ptraci, who was to be entombed with the king, setting himself against Dios and the whole machinery of tradition.

The Great Pyramid raised for the dead king is far larger than any before it, and pyramids in Djelibeybi store and release enormous quantities of time. When the new pyramid is completed and flares, it warps space so violently that the entire kingdom is twisted out of the ordinary world into a dimension of its own. Cut off, Djelibeybi finds that all the gods its people ever believed in have suddenly become real and walk the land, quarrelling and causing chaos. Teppic, who was outside the kingdom with Ptraci when it vanished, must find a way back in, while Dios's true, ancient nature and the pyramid's role in preserving the kingdom's frozen way of life come to light.

Teppic returns to the displaced kingdom and, with Ptraci, the builder Ptaclusp, and others, works out that the Great Pyramid must be destroyed to release its stored time and let Djelibeybi rejoin the world. They succeed in discharging and collapsing it; the pocket dimension folds away, the manifested gods vanish, and the kingdom returns to reality. Dios, caught in the pyramid's final flare, is flung thousands of years into the past, to the founding of the kingdom, doomed to begin his endless service over again. Teppic, now king, recognizes that Djelibeybi cannot go on frozen in time. He abdicates in favour of Ptraci, who is revealed to be his half-sister and who becomes queen, opening the kingdom to the outside world and ending the age of pyramids. His father's restless spirit is finally laid to rest.

characters.description: Queen of Terrasen, back in Rifthold under her own name at last, with fire magic she can now control and a very short list of objectives: free her cousin Aedion from the dungeons before he is executed, break the collar on Dorian Havilliard, kill the king of Adarlan, and get the Wyrdkeys away from him. She has spent ten years as the assassin Celaena Sardothien and is not sure how much of that woman she is willing to give up. She is imperious, theatrical, and hard on the people who care about her, and she is carrying more grief and more debt than she will admit.
characters.name: Aelin Ashryver Galathynius

characters.description: A Fae warrior of Doranelle, centuries old, blood-sworn to Aelin and the first member of her court. He has wind and ice magic, can take the shape of a hawk, and is very much out of place in a mortal city where magic does not work. He is the only person Aelin does not perform for.
characters.name: Rowan Whitethorn

characters.description: Formerly Captain of the Royal Guard, now a hunted man living rough with the rebels in Rifthold, working to free Dorian and to keep the resistance alive. He has lost his position, his oath, and most of his certainties, and he blames himself for what happened to the prince. The woman who comes back from Wendlyn is not the one he sent away, and he does not know how to speak to her.
characters.name: Chaol Westfall

characters.description: A former city guard of Rifthold, a baker's daughter of southern continent descent and a superb archer, now fully committed to the rebellion and working alongside Chaol. She is direct, unsentimental, and unimpressed by titles.
characters.name: Nesryn Faliq

characters.description: Crown Prince of Adarlan, wearing a collar of black Wyrdstone that has given a demon prince out of the Wyrdgate the use of his body. What walks the castle in his shape speaks with borrowed courtesy, hunts rebels for his father, and shows no recognition of anyone the prince knew. Whether anything of Dorian is still inside is an open question.
characters.name: Dorian Havilliard

characters.description: The ruler of Adarlan, who holds at least one Wyrdkey and whose black-stone towers have kept magic dead on this continent for a decade. He has collared his own son and is preparing something at Duke Perrington's fortress in the south. He is patient, unhurried, and has never yet been surprised.
characters.name: The King of Adarlan

characters.description: General of the Bane and Aelin's cousin, chained in the castle dungeons and condemned to public execution for treason. He spent ten years pretending to serve Adarlan while keeping Terrasen's legion intact for a queen he was never certain had survived. He is proud, reckless, and physically wrecked by his imprisonment.
characters.name: Aedion Ashryver

characters.description: King of the Assassins and master of Rifthold's guild, the man who bought Aelin as a child, trained her, and made her what she is. Elegant, generous, and utterly controlling, he greets her return as a homecoming and offers his help. Every gift he gives is a debt, and both of them know it.
characters.name: Arobynn Hamel

characters.description: Rifthold's most sought-after courtesan, beautiful and superbly poised, who was sold into the trade as a child and has spent years surviving Arobynn Hamel's household. She and Aelin were rivals long ago and remember it differently. She is raising an orphaned girl named Evangeline and has her own reasons for wanting Arobynn Hamel's household dismantled.
characters.name: Lysandra

characters.description: A scarred girl of about ten with a badly injured face, taken in by Lysandra and treated by her as a daughter.
characters.name: Evangeline

characters.description: Wing Leader of the Ironteeth host, commanding the aerial legions from Duke Perrington's fortress at Morath. She has a wyvern named Abraxos, iron teeth and nails, and a coven of thirteen witches who follow her without question. She is being given orders whose purpose is never explained, and for the first time in a century of obedience she is beginning to want explanations.
characters.name: Manon Blackbeak

characters.description: Manon's Second and cousin, the best flier in the Thirteen and the only one who will tell Manon when she is wrong. She carries something she has never spoken about.
characters.name: Asterin Blackbeak

characters.description: The king's chief commander and lord of Morath, the black fortress in the southern mountains where the wyverns were bred and where the Ironteeth are quartered. He has begun projects in the lower levels that even the witches are not shown, and he wears a ring of black stone.
characters.name: Duke Perrington

characters.description: A young woman working as a servant in the kitchens of Morath, thin and quiet, one ankle shattered and braced from a childhood injury. She is the daughter of Terrasen's Lady of Perranth and was raised in a tower under lock and key by the uncle who took her mother's lands. She hears everything the fortress says and repeats none of it.
characters.name: Elide Lochan

characters.description: Lord of Perranth by Adarlan's grant, having taken the title from his brother's family after the conquest. He is at Morath in the duke's service, watching his niece with an interest that is not familial concern.
characters.name: Vernon Lochan

characters.description: Once an ambitious lady of the Rifthold court, now kept at Morath in a haze of opium and worse, wearing a black ring the duke gave her. She is barely lucid, watched constantly, and used for purposes she cannot describe.
characters.name: Kaltain Rompier

characters.description: The first Queen of Adarlan, dead a thousand years, whose spirit has been steering Aelin toward this confrontation since the beginning. She appears again with instructions, and with rather less of an explanation than Aelin now demands.
characters.name: Elena Galathynius

recaps.ending: The king of Adarlan is dead, killed by his own son once Dorian throws off the collar, and with his last words he claims he too was a puppet of the Valg, taken over long ago. Aelin destroys what remains of the glass castle, and magic is free across the continent for the first time in a decade. Chaol is left with a broken back and no feeling in his legs. Dorian is King of Adarlan, alone, holding a ruined capital and a country his father wrecked. Aelin, Rowan, Aedion, Lysandra, and Evangeline ride north for Terrasen, where Aelin has a kingdom to reclaim, an army she does not have, and lords who may not accept her. She carries the Amulet of Orynth and the Wyrdkey inside it, and she knows the third key is still at large. Chaol and Nesryn sail for the southern continent, to the healers of the Torre Cesme in Antica, to seek both a cure and an alliance. At Morath, Kaltain Rompier destroys herself and a great deal of the fortress, pressing a shard of Wyrdstone into Elide Lochan's hand and telling her to find Celaena Sardothien; Elide escapes into the countryside alone. Manon, cast out and wounded for defying her grandmother, is left with the Thirteen and a set of questions about her own history she has never been allowed to ask. Erawan, the Valg king who was never truly dead, is now unopposed at Morath.
recaps.in_short: Aelin Galathynius returns to Rifthold with Rowan to free her condemned cousin Aedion, break the Valg collar on Dorian, and kill the king of Adarlan. Reclaiming her old life brings her back to Arobynn Hamel, the assassin master who raised her, whose help costs more than it is worth, and to Lysandra, a courtesan who turns out to be a shapeshifter and becomes her closest ally. Aelin frees Aedion in a public rescue, has Arobynn killed, and inherits his fortune and the Amulet of Orynth, which proves to contain the third Wyrdkey. At Morath, the witch Manon Blackbeak is shown what the duke is breeding in the lower levels, begins to refuse her orders, and saves a servant named Elide Lochan. In Rifthold, Aelin destroys the black tower holding magic down, restoring it across the continent, then confronts the king; Dorian breaks the collar and kills his father, at the cost of a magical blast that shatters Chaol's spine. Aelin brings down the glass castle. Dorian takes the throne, Chaol and Nesryn sail south for healing and allies, and Aelin turns north to claim Terrasen against a war that is only beginning.

recaps.text: Previously: the assassin Celaena Sardothien served a year as the King of Adarlan's Champion before admitting that she is Aelin Ashryver Galathynius, the lost heir of Terrasen. Sent overseas to Wendlyn, she was taken in hand by the Fae warrior Rowan Whitethorn on the orders of Queen Maeve, mastered the fire magic she had spent her life hiding from, and faced her family's murder and her own guilt. She learned that the king of Adarlan holds at least one of the three Wyrdkeys, fragments of a shattered gate between worlds, and that his soldiers carry Valg demons inside them, bound by collars and rings of black Wyrdstone. After destroying such a force at the fortress of Mistward, she declared herself queen, refused Maeve's blood oath, and won Rowan's instead. In Rifthold, everything went wrong while she was away: her cousin Aedion Ashryver, secretly loyal to Terrasen all along, was arrested for treason and condemned; the healer Sorscha was executed; Chaol Westfall was driven out of the castle into hiding with the rebels; and Dorian Havilliard, exposed as a magic-wielder, was collared by his father and is now ridden by a Valg prince. In the north, the Ironteeth witch Manon Blackbeak was made Wing Leader of an aerial army raised for a war nobody has explained.

Aelin arrives back in Rifthold with Rowan and begins working the city, killing the king's Valg-ridden guards and learning how much has changed. Chaol and Nesryn are living underground with the rebels; the reunion between Aelin and Chaol is cold, because she has come back as a queen with priorities and he has spent months believing he ruined everything. Aedion is in the castle dungeons, beaten and starving, condemned to be executed publicly on the king's birthday, days away. Dorian, or the thing wearing him, hunts rebels for his father and does not appear to recognize anyone. Needing money, information, and the resources of the city's underworld, Aelin goes back to the one person she swore never to see again: Arobynn Hamel, the King of the Assassins, who raised her, sold her, and greets her return as though nothing happened. At Morath, Manon Blackbeak commands the Ironteeth legions for Duke Perrington and is increasingly aware that the fortress is doing something in its lower levels that she has not been shown.

Arobynn agrees to help free Aedion, at a price, and Aelin agrees to it knowing she is being played. Through him she is drawn back into the world of the guild and reunited with Lysandra, the courtesan she once treated as a rival, who has spent years in Arobynn's household and has more reason to hate him than Aelin does. The two become allies and then friends. Rowan, magicless in Rifthold and conspicuous, keeps close to Aelin and takes an instant dislike to almost everyone. Aelin and Chaol argue about what she has become, about Dorian, and about whether the prince can be saved at all; Chaol insists he is still in there, Aelin is not convinced anything is left to save. Meanwhile Aelin scouts the castle, revisits the tunnels and Elena's tomb beneath it, and starts assembling a plan to take Aedion off the execution block in front of the entire court.

The rescue works: Aelin, Rowan, Chaol, Nesryn, and their allies pull Aedion out of the execution and get him clear of the castle. Aedion, half dead and ten years past believing it possible, meets his cousin again and swears the blood oath to her, becoming the second member of her court. The group holes up in a warehouse in the slums while Aedion recovers and the plans grow: free Dorian, break the towers of black stone that hold magic down, kill the king. At Morath, Duke Perrington finally shows Manon what is being done in the fortress: Ironteeth witches of the Yellowlegs clan are being used to breed something with the Valg, and the results are not witches. Manon is ordered to approve of it. She meets a quiet, limping kitchen servant named Elide Lochan, a Terrasen girl kept there by her uncle Vernon, and finds herself doing something she cannot justify to her grandmother: leaving the girl alive and noticed.

Lysandra reveals what she has hidden all her life: she is a shapeshifter, her magic bound and stolen from her since childhood, and with magic still dead in Rifthold she can do nothing with it at all. She and Aelin become genuine allies rather than convenient ones. Elena's spirit presses Aelin again about the Wyrdkeys and the gate, and Aelin, tired of being steered by a thousand-year-old ghost with an agenda, demands answers she does not get. Arobynn's help comes due, and the price he actually wants becomes clear; Aelin begins arranging how to settle with him rather than pay it. Her plan sharpens around the black towers: bring one down and magic returns to the whole continent, which is the only way any of them can fight the king at all. Chaol, thinking about a city full of collared Valg soldiers who would also get their power back, argues hard against it.

Aelin settles her account with Arobynn Hamel permanently: he dies at the hands of someone in his own household, and his fortune, his guild, and his effects pass to her. She is suddenly one of the wealthiest people in Rifthold, which is what an assault on a castle costs. Aedion, Rowan, Lysandra, Chaol, and Nesryn each take a piece of the plan. At Morath, Manon is ordered to prove her obedience in ways she can no longer stomach, and the Thirteen begin to notice their leader hesitating. Elide, aware that her uncle intends to use her for the duke's purposes, prepares to run and hoards what she can. Kaltain Rompier, kept drugged and half-conscious in the tower, watches everything and is written off by everyone as broken. Rifthold's streets fill with the king's Valg guards and the rebels are hunted down one cell at a time, and the timetable collapses: the strike has to happen soon.

Among the things that came to Aelin from Arobynn's estate is the Amulet of Orynth, her family's ancient talisman, which he had kept as leverage over her for years. She works out what it actually is: the third Wyrdkey, hidden inside it for a thousand years and worn around her own neck without her knowing. At Morath, Manon defies the fortress outright, cutting Elide loose and getting her out with a warning to head north and find Celaena Sardothien. Her grandmother punishes the defiance viciously, and the Thirteen close ranks around her; Manon begins to suspect that the story she was told about her own mother is a lie. In Rifthold, Aelin and Chaol have their reckoning, sorting out what they were to each other and what they are now, and part on honest terms. Aelin and Rowan stop pretending about each other. The assault on the glass castle begins.

The tower falls and magic returns across the continent all at once, slamming back into everyone who ever had it. Lysandra takes another shape for the first time in years. Rowan has his power back. Every collared Valg soldier in Rifthold becomes far more dangerous, and the city descends into a running battle. Aelin fights her way through the glass castle to the throne room, where the king waits with the Wyrdkeys and with Dorian at his side. Chaol goes with her, refusing to leave the prince behind. What is wearing Dorian is stronger than any of them expected, and the king turns his son on his own friends. The confrontation becomes a contest of will over Dorian's body, with Chaol pleading with a friend who shows no sign of hearing him.

Dorian breaks the collar. Something of him has survived after all, and reaching for Chaol is what does it. He turns on his father and kills him, and the dying king claims he was himself taken over by the Valg long ago, that everything Adarlan has done was done by the thing inside him, and that a far older enemy is coming. The magic loosed in the throne room shatters Chaol's spine, leaving him alive but unable to move his legs. Aelin brings the glass castle down. In the ruins, Dorian is king of a broken empire; Aelin holds the Amulet of Orynth and the key inside it and knows the third remains at Morath, where the Valg king Erawan has been waiting all along. At Morath, Kaltain Rompier finally acts, destroying herself and much of the fortress, and pressing a shard of Wyrdstone into Elide Lochan's hand before she goes.

Rifthold is left half-ruined and leaderless until Dorian takes the throne, with Aelin's promise of alliance and very little else. Chaol, unable to walk, refuses to be a burden and sails for Antica on the southern continent with Nesryn Faliq, to seek the healers of the Torre Cesme and, more importantly, an army from the khaganate. Aelin, Rowan, Aedion, Lysandra, and Evangeline turn north for Terrasen, a kingdom Aelin has not seen in ten years, whose lords have no reason to hand a throne to a girl they last saw as a child and who has been an assassin ever since. Elide Lochan is on the road alone, hunted, carrying Kaltain's shard and a name to find. Manon Blackbeak commands the Ironteeth at a cost her grandmother has begun to count, with the truth about her own bloodline still hidden from her. Erawan's armies are intact, his creatures are multiplying, and the war for the continent has not yet begun.

characters.description: Mistress of Ingleside, home again at Glen St. Mary after three months abroad with Gilbert. Her children are growing up and need her less, and she watches the doings of the Glen, and of the new minister's family in particular, with sympathy rather than interference. She is content and no longer at the centre of her own story.
characters.name: Anne Blythe

characters.description: The Ingleside housekeeper, devoted to the Blythes and to their standing in the Glen, an authority on every family in the district and a reliable source of the news, the gossip, and the moral verdict that goes with it.
characters.name: Susan Baker

characters.description: Once Miss Cornelia Bryant of Four Winds, now married and living at the Glen, still capable, still blunt, and still convinced that men are a trial. She takes a practical interest in the neglected manse family and does more for them than the whole congregation put together.
characters.name: Mrs. Marshall Elliott

characters.description: The eldest Blythe boy, red-haired, energetic, and full of plans, who leads the children's expeditions and intends to be a soldier or an explorer or whatever else the week suggests.
characters.name: Jem Blythe

characters.description: The second Blythe boy, beautiful and dreamy, who writes verses, loves words and the look of the world, and shrinks from ugliness and violence. The other boys of the Glen think him soft; his own family know that he sees and feels more than the rest of them.
characters.name: Walter Blythe

characters.description: One of the Blythe twins, dark-eyed and serious, close to Faith and Una Meredith and inclined to take the manse children's troubles as her own.
characters.name: Nan Blythe

characters.description: Nan's twin, red-haired and quick-tempered, Jem's usual companion in the games and expeditions of Rainbow Valley.
characters.name: Di Blythe

characters.description: The youngest Blythe, a small, pretty girl who lisps, minds her clothes, and dislikes being laughed at, tagging after the older children in the valley.
characters.name: Rilla Blythe

characters.description: The new Presbyterian minister at Glen St. Mary, a widower with four children, scholarly, unworldly, and so absorbed in his books and his sermons that he does not notice the state of his house or the behaviour of his family. He is beloved in the pulpit and helpless everywhere else.
characters.name: Rev. John Meredith

characters.description: The eldest Meredith child, a sensible, self-appointed leader of his brother and sisters, quick to see when they have gone too far and equally quick to have gone there with them.
characters.name: Jerry Meredith

characters.description: The elder Meredith daughter, warm-hearted, fearless, and entirely without discretion, who acts on impulse and cannot understand why the Glen is scandalized by things that seemed perfectly reasonable at the time. She is fiercely proud of her father.
characters.name: Faith Meredith

characters.description: The younger Meredith daughter, quiet, anxious, and easily hurt, who worries about her father and her family's reputation and keeps her thoughts to herself. She is the one who notices when other people are unhappy.
characters.name: Una Meredith

characters.description: The youngest Meredith, a boy with his mother's blue eyes who collects insects, frogs, and snakes and keeps them about his person, to the horror of the congregation.
characters.name: Carl Meredith

characters.description: The Merediths' elderly housekeeper, half blind and nearly deaf, who nursed their father as a baby and will let no one else near the kitchen. Her cooking and her housekeeping are equally bad, and Mr. Meredith will not hear of dismissing her.
characters.name: Aunt Martha

characters.description: A half-starved runaway girl of about twelve found hiding in an abandoned barn, sharp-tongued, worldly, and free with information the manse children have never heard before. She has been passed from one hard household to another and has learned to look out for herself.
characters.name: Mary Vance

characters.description: One of two sisters living at a house up the hill above the harbour, a gentle, fair woman no longer young, who keeps house with her elder sister and is well liked in the Glen. She and the minister fall into conversation one evening and find they suit each other.
characters.name: Rosemary West

characters.description: Rosemary's elder sister, dark, heavy-browed, and dominant, devoted to Rosemary and determined that the two of them shall never be parted.
characters.name: Ellen West

characters.description: A loud, red-bearded, prosperous farmer of the district, famous for his temper, his opinions, and his long absence from church, who says whatever comes into his head at whatever volume it arrives.
characters.name: Norman Douglas

recaps.ending: Norman Douglas returns to church and to his old courtship of Ellen West, and the two become engaged. Ellen, marrying herself, releases Rosemary from the promise that had kept her single, and Rosemary accepts John Meredith. Una Meredith, who has been dreading a stepmother more than she could say, goes alone to Rosemary to ask her to be kind to Carl, and comes away comforted; the manse children accept the marriage and gain the mothering they have gone without. Mr. Meredith, shaken by how far his family had been neglected, is at last awake to his household. Mary Vance is settled with Mrs. Marshall Elliott and thoroughly at home in the Glen. The Blythe and Meredith children are all a year or two older, and Rainbow Valley is still theirs. The book closes with them gathered in the valley at sunset, where Walter tells them he has seen the Pied Piper coming over the hills with his music, calling the boys of the world to follow him. The others take it for one of Walter's fancies and promise lightly to follow when the call comes, and the story ends on that promise with the shadow of the coming war lying over it.
recaps.in_short: A new Presbyterian minister, the scholarly and unworldly John Meredith, comes to Glen St. Mary with four motherless children and an incompetent old housekeeper, and the manse family runs wild. Jerry, Faith, Una, and Carl make friends with the Blythe children of Ingleside and spend their days in Rainbow Valley, scandalizing the congregation with one thoughtless escapade after another while their father reads in his study and notices nothing. They rescue a starving runaway, Mary Vance, who is eventually taken in and brought up by Mrs. Marshall Elliott. Ashamed of disgracing their father, the manse children form a club to punish their own misdeeds, and one of the punishments makes Carl seriously ill, which finally wakes Mr. Meredith to his family's neglect. Meanwhile he falls in love with Rosemary West, who must refuse him because of a promise never to marry, extracted by her sister Ellen. When Ellen's own old suitor returns and marries her, Rosemary is freed and accepts the minister. The book ends with Walter Blythe's vision of the Pied Piper, a warning of the war to come.

recaps.text: Previously: Anne Shirley, brought up as an orphan at Green Gables in Avonlea, married Doctor Gilbert Blythe and lives at Ingleside in Glen St. Mary with their housekeeper Susan Baker and their children, Jem, Walter, the twins Nan and Di, Shirley, and the youngest, Rilla. Their neighbour and old friend from Four Winds days, once Miss Cornelia Bryant, is now Mrs. Marshall Elliott and lives at the Glen. The doctor's practice is long established and the family well settled. In this book Anne and Gilbert step back into the background: the story belongs to their children and to the family of the new minister at the Glen manse, and the setting is the wooded hollow below Ingleside that the children have named Rainbow Valley.

Anne comes home to Ingleside after three months in Europe, and the Glen catches her up on its news, chiefly the new Presbyterian minister. John Meredith is a widower with four children, a fine preacher, and hopelessly unpractical: the manse is dirty and disorderly, the meals are ruinous, and his old housekeeper, Aunt Martha, is half blind and will not be dismissed. Jerry, Faith, Una, and Carl Meredith are left to bring themselves up, and they do it cheerfully, running about the graveyard beside the church and making friends at once with the Blythe children in Rainbow Valley, the wooded hollow below Ingleside. Exploring an abandoned barn, the children find a half-starved girl of about twelve hiding there. Mary Vance has run away from a hard mistress and has nowhere to go; the manse children feed her and take her in, without troubling to consult their father.

Mary Vance is installed at the manse, where she is useful, sharp-tongued, and a good deal too well informed for the taste of the Glen. Her situation is settled when it emerges that the woman she ran from cannot claim her, and Mrs. Marshall Elliott takes her to bring up, giving Mary a home and the Glen a steady supply of comment. The manse children go on disgracing their father without meaning to: they play in the graveyard, keep house on the wrong day, and appear at church in whatever they happen to be wearing, and the congregation talks. Mr. Meredith, absorbed in his books, sees none of it. Walking home one evening he falls into conversation with Rosemary West, one of two sisters who keep house up the hill, and finds himself talking easily for the first time since his wife died. He begins to visit the hill house, and Ellen West watches the friendship with growing unease.

The manse children learn how badly the Glen speaks of them and are horrified, less for themselves than for their father, and they form a club to keep themselves in order, with the rule that any of them who does wrong shall choose and carry out their own punishment. The penalties are as ill-judged as the offences: they go without meals, walk to church in disgrace, and set themselves ordeals no adult would have permitted. Faith goes on acting first and thinking afterwards, in one case riding a neighbour's pig through the village for a wager, and afterwards, when the congregation blames her father for her behaviour, standing up in church to explain herself to the whole assembly, which scandalizes the Glen more than the original offence. Walter Blythe, who hates fighting, fights an older boy who has insulted Faith and his own mother, and is respected afterwards by boys who had thought him a coward.

John Meredith at last asks Rosemary West to marry him. She refuses, and cannot tell him why: years ago, when Ellen gave up her own chance of marriage to keep house for her sister, Rosemary promised never to leave her. The minister, humiliated and baffled, keeps away from the hill house, and Rosemary is left as unhappy as he is. When she tells Ellen what she has given up, the two sisters quarrel and settle into a cold silence. Faith and Una, learning something of the courtship, are torn between wanting their father happy and dreading a stepmother, and Una in particular is wretched about it. The manse runs on as badly as ever, and Mary Vance, from her comfortable place with Mrs. Marshall Elliott, keeps the children supplied with the Glen's opinion of them.

One of the club's self-imposed penalties goes badly wrong. Carl, punishing himself for a fault, spends a whole night alone in the graveyard in the cold, is brought home ill, and his illness turns dangerous. His father, sitting up with him, understands for the first time how far he has let his children go untended, and is bitterly ashamed of it. Carl recovers, and Mr. Meredith is a better father afterwards for the shock of it. Into this comes Norman Douglas, a loud, red-bearded farmer who has stayed away from church for years and who takes it into his head to come back, and to renew a courtship he abandoned in his youth.

Norman Douglas courts Ellen West as noisily as he does everything else, and Ellen, who refused him long ago, accepts him. Marrying herself, she can no longer hold Rosemary to the promise she exacted, and she releases her outright. Rosemary and John Meredith are reconciled and engaged, and the manse is to have a mistress at last. Una Meredith, still frightened of what a stepmother may mean, goes alone to Rosemary to beg her to be good to Carl, and Rosemary's answer settles the children's fears. Mary Vance is at home with Mrs. Marshall Elliott and as talkative as ever. On a still evening the children gather in Rainbow Valley, and Walter tells them that he has seen the Pied Piper coming down over the hills, playing, and that one day he will call and the boys will have to follow him. The others laugh and promise to go when the call comes, and the book ends there.
